title: Research the market
description:
A good starting point when you want to prepare yourself for negotiating your salary in an interview is to do some research first.

You should search for what is the average salary for this position in your country / city.

Some websites such as Indeed or Glassdoor gather the average salary for different companies, so if the one you are applying for is there, it is worth it to check out how much people in the same position were being paid when they worked in that company.

title: Focus on what you can offer
description:
Another really important thing to keep in mind is what you have accomplished in your carrer.

 Your salary should reflect how much time of experience you have, your education and your impact in past projects.

 Many people forget to consider these factors when finding an acceptable range for their salary and they are for sure the most relevant part.

title: Timing matters
description:
One of the biggest mistakes people make is bringing up salary too early in the interview process. If you mention money in the first interview, it can give the impression that you only care about the paycheck and not about the role itself.

The best moment to discuss salary is usually after the company has already shown strong interest in hiring you, typically in the final rounds or when they bring it up themselves.

By waiting for the right moment, you put yourself in a much stronger position because the company has already invested time and effort into your candidacy, which means they are more likely to meet your expectations.

title: Let them say the number first
description:
Whenever possible, try to let the interviewer or recruiter be the first one to mention a number. When you say a number first, you risk either underselling yourself or scaring them away with a figure that is too high.

If they ask you directly what salary you are expecting, you can redirect by saying something like "I would love to hear more about the compensation range you have in mind for this position" or "I am flexible and would like to understand the full scope of the role first."

This way, you get to hear their range before committing to anything, and you can then negotiate from a position where you already know what they are willing to pay.

title: Use a specific number
description:
When the time comes to actually say a number, try to avoid round numbers like $50,000 or $80,000. Instead, use a more specific figure like $52,500 or $78,400.

This might seem like a small detail, but research shows that specific numbers make the other person believe you have done your homework and that there is a real reason behind that exact figure. Round numbers, on the other hand, feel arbitrary and are easier to negotiate down.

Of course, this number should still be based on your actual research and experience, but framing it as a precise amount gives you a psychological advantage during the conversation.

title: Look beyond the base salary
description:
Salary negotiation is not only about the monthly or annual paycheck. Many companies offer additional benefits that can significantly increase your total compensation, and sometimes these are even easier to negotiate than the base salary itself.

Things like health insurance, remote work flexibility, extra vacation days, stock options, annual bonuses, professional development budgets and relocation assistance are all part of the package. Before the negotiation, make a list of what matters most to you beyond the base salary.

If the company cannot meet your salary expectation, you can ask about improving other parts of the offer. For example, an extra week of paid vacation or the option to work remotely a few days per week can be just as valuable as a higher salary depending on your priorities.

title: Key phrases for negotiating
description:
Having a set of professional phrases ready for the negotiation moment is incredibly helpful, especially if English is not your first language. The right words can make you sound confident and reasonable at the same time.

Some useful phrases include: "Based on my research and experience, I was expecting something in the range of..." or "I really appreciate this offer. Is there any flexibility on the base salary?" or "I am very excited about this opportunity and I would love to find a number that works for both of us."

Avoid phrases that sound too aggressive like "I need more money" or too passive like "Whatever you think is fair." The goal is to sound like someone who knows their worth but is also collaborative and open to discussion.

title: How to counter a low offer
description:
Receiving an offer that is below your expectations can be disappointing, but how you react to it makes all the difference. The worst thing you can do is accept it on the spot out of fear, or reject it emotionally.

Instead, take a moment and respond with something like: "Thank you for the offer, I am really excited about this role. Based on my experience and the market research I have done, I was hoping for something closer to [your target number]. Is there room to discuss this further?"

This approach shows gratitude, reaffirms your interest in the position, and opens the door for a constructive conversation. Most companies expect candidates to negotiate, so a low initial offer does not necessarily mean they are unwilling to go higher.

title: Dodge the "current salary" question
description:
One of the trickiest questions you can face during a salary negotiation is "What is your current salary?" or "How much are you making right now?" This question can put you at a disadvantage because if your current salary is low, it anchors the new offer to that number.

A good way to handle this is by redirecting the conversation to your expectations instead. You can say something like: "I would prefer to focus on the value I can bring to this role and what the market rate is for this position" or "I am looking for a salary in the range of [X] based on my skills and experience."

In many places, employers are actually not allowed to ask this question by law. But even where it is legal, you are never obligated to answer. Keeping the focus on what you are worth rather than what you were paid before is always the smarter strategy.

title: Practice your delivery
description:
It is one thing to know what number you want and another thing entirely to say it out loud with confidence. Many people freeze or sound unsure when the moment comes to actually state their salary expectation, and that hesitation can weaken your position.

Before the interview, practice saying your target salary out loud multiple times. Stand in front of a mirror, record yourself, or ask a friend to role-play the conversation with you. The goal is to say the number as naturally and calmly as if you were stating your name.

Your tone of voice, your pace and your body language all communicate confidence. If you say "I am looking for seventy-five thousand" while making eye contact and speaking at a steady pace, it carries much more weight than mumbling the same number while looking away.

title: Get everything in writing
description:
Verbal promises during the interview process can feel reassuring, but they mean very little if they are not documented in your official offer letter or contract. Always make sure that everything you negotiated is clearly written down before you accept.

This includes not only your base salary but also any bonuses, equity, benefits, start date, job title and any special arrangements like remote work or flexible hours that were discussed. If something was promised verbally but is missing from the written offer, ask politely for it to be included.

It might feel awkward to ask for these details in writing, but it is a completely normal and professional thing to do. It protects both you and the company from misunderstandings down the road.

title: Know when to stop
description:
Negotiation is a skill, but knowing when you have reached the best possible outcome is equally important. Pushing too hard or going back and forth too many times can damage the relationship with your future employer before you even start.

A good sign that you have reached the limit is when the recruiter or hiring manager says something like "This is the best we can do" or "We have reached the top of our budget for this role." At that point, continuing to push is unlikely to get you a better result and might make them reconsider the offer entirely.

Once you feel satisfied with the overall package or sense that the company has genuinely reached their limit, accept gracefully. Thank them for their flexibility and express your excitement about joining. Starting the job on a positive note is worth just as much as the extra money you negotiated.
